nameStory: The milk snail gets its common name from its creamy white or pale shell that resembles the color of milk. This large Mediterranean native is also called the Spanish snail, reflecting its abundance in Spain and other parts of southern Europe where it's been harvested as food for thousands of years.
description: The milk snail is a large, air-breathing land snail with a distinctive pale, creamy shell that can grow quite substantial in size. Unlike our native New England snails, this Mediterranean species has a robust, globe-shaped shell with prominent spiral ridges. It's an edible species that belongs to the same family as the famous French escargot snails. These terrestrial mollusks are extremely rare visitors to New England, with only a couple of confirmed sightings.

idTips.label: Shell Color and Pattern
idTips.description: The shell is predominantly creamy white to pale yellow, often with faint brown spiral bands that may be barely visible or completely absent, giving it that characteristic milky appearance

idTips.label: Shell Size and Shape
idTips.description: Much larger than native New England snails, with a robust, globe-shaped shell that feels substantial and heavy when picked up

idTips.label: Shell Texture
idTips.description: The shell surface has a smooth, slightly chalky feel with distinct growth ridges that you can run your finger across

idTips.label: Shell Opening
idTips.description: The shell opening (aperture) is large and oval-shaped with a thick, white rim that feels smooth to the touch

idTips.label: Overall Appearance
idTips.description: When active, the snail's body is typically grayish and much larger than our common garden snails, extending well beyond what you'd expect from native species

habitat: Milk snails are extremely rare in New England and are not established here naturally. Any sightings would likely be in urban areas, possibly near ports or in gardens where they might have arrived accidentally with imported plants or goods. They prefer Mediterranean-type climates with mild, wet winters and dry summers, so New England's harsh winters make long-term survival unlikely.

seasonality.spring: If present, milk snails would become active as temperatures warm, emerging from winter hiding spots to feed on fresh vegetation.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when these snails would be most visible, though they may seek shelter during the hottest, driest days.
seasonality.fall: Active feeding continues as they prepare for winter dormancy, potentially the best time to spot any individuals before they hide.
seasonality.winter: Would likely be hidden under debris, rocks, or deep soil layers, essentially inactive and very difficult to find in New England's harsh winters.

funFact: Ancient Romans were harvesting and eating milk snails over 2,000 years ago at archaeological sites in Morocco, making this one of humanity's longest continuously harvested gastropod species - and they're still considered a delicacy in Mediterranean countries today!
confusionNotes: In New England, a milk snail would be unmistakable due to its large size and pale coloration - our native snails are much smaller and typically darker brown. The main confusion would be distinguishing it from other large European snail species that might occasionally appear as hitchhikers, but the milk snail's characteristic creamy-white shell makes it distinctive.
contextualKnowledge: The milk snail represents one of many Mediterranean species that occasionally appear in North American ports and cities as accidental introductions, but unlike some invasive snails, it hasn't established populations in our climate. Any sighting in New England would be noteworthy and worth reporting to local naturalists.
compareHints: Since there are no other Otala species in New England, compare the milk snail to other large European snails in the Helicidae family that might occasionally appear here. The milk snail's pale, milky coloration and substantial size distinguish it from the typically darker brown garden snails and smaller native species. Its smooth, chalky shell texture and thick white aperture rim are key features that separate it from other large land snails.
